description: Team Cassiopeia is a passionate team exploring astronomy, space science, and technology. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we aim to build an interactive web tool that makes SPHEREx observations accessible, allowing users to explore how objects in the sky change in position and brightness over time.
summary:
Cassiopeia: SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a public-facing web app that helps people explore real infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users enter sky coordinates, search NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), and view matching observations as a chronological animation. They can compare two dates, inspect image metadata and quality flags, explore light-curve and motion-tracking estimates, and save notes about what they observe.

The app addresses the challenge by making it easier to see how a patch of sky changes over time. Its guided workflow and beginner resources help people engage with genuine astronomy data without needing to download and process FITS files manually. This matters because an accessible view can help students and the public investigate possible changes in the sky and learn how scientists work with observations. The app supports exploration, not confirmed discoveries: its measurements are preliminary, and saved findings are not automatically sent to researchers.
details:
Cassiopeia: SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a public-facing web app for exploring real infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users enter sky coordinates, search NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), and view available observations in chronological order. They can animate images, compare two dates, inspect observation metadata and quality flags, explore a light curve or candidate motion track, and save notes for download.

The app makes archive data easier to approach for students and members of the public who may not have experience handling astronomy files. Its intended impact is to help more people inspect how a patch of sky appears across observation dates and learn how astronomers work with infrared data. The app supports investigation; its exploratory measurements do not confirm a discovery, and saved notes are not submitted to scientists.

We developed the application in Python using Streamlit for the web interface, Astroquery and direct HTTP requests to access IRSA services, and Astropy for FITS files, coordinates, units, time, and WCS operations. NumPy, Matplotlib, and the reproject package support image processing, plots, and alignment. The project uses no special hardware; it runs as a web application and retrieves public archive data over the internet.

Cassiopeia’s creative element is its guided, time-based view of real SPHEREx observations, paired with beginner explanations and optional analysis tools. We considered data availability, slow archive responses, image quality flags, changing wavelengths, image alignment, uncertainty, and the need to avoid presenting preliminary visual patterns as confirmed science.
